questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A sports club's total market value of all final goods and services produced within its stadium district in one year is best described as?

options.text: Gross domestic product for that district

options.misconception: confuses domestic location with national ownership

questions.explanation: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a geographic area in a period. GNP and income concepts differ.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A club buys leather for $200 and sells a finished ball for $500. How much of this counts in GDP?

options.misconception: confuses value added with final sale

questions.explanation: GDP counts the final good at $500. Adding the intermediate leather would double count its value.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A stadium vendor buys dough for $30 and sells pretzels for $80. What is the value added?
questions.explanation: Value added is sale price minus intermediate cost, or 80 minus 30 equals 50. This avoids double counting.
questions.hint: Subtract input cost from sale price.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Value added and the final good
questions.learningObjective: Relate value added to final value
questions.stem: Explain why summing value added across all stages equals the final good's price.

answer.exemplar: Each stage's value added captures only its contribution; summing them telescopes to the final price because intermediate costs cancel out.

questions.explanation: Value added at each stage nets out intermediate purchases, so the sum equals the final good's market price.
questions.hint: Intermediate costs cancel in the sum.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A fan resells a used ticket for $80 that was originally bought for $50. How is this treated in GDP?

options.text: Not counted, as it is a second-hand sale

questions.explanation: Second-hand sales transfer existing goods and are not new production. Only broker services on the resale count.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Which formula sums the expenditure approach to GDP for a sports economy?

options.misconception: uses national income instead of net exports

questions.explanation: The expenditure approach is C + I + G + (X - M), written as C + I + G + NX. Other formulas measure different things.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A club builds a new training facility. In GDP accounting this is?

options.misconception: treats capital spending as a transfer

questions.explanation: New construction of a capital good counts as investment in the accounts. It is not consumption, government spending, or a transfer.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A city gives a $1 million grant to a sports club for youth programs. In GDP accounting, is this government spending on goods and services?

options.misconception: treats the grant as direct production

options.text: Yes, because the government spent money
options.misconception: confuses any outlay with a purchase

options.text: No, it is a transfer payment

options.misconception: gives the right answer for the wrong reason

questions.explanation: A grant is a transfer payment, not a purchase of goods or services, so it is not in G. Only direct government purchases count.
questions.hint: Was a good or service produced in return?

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A club exports $120 million in merchandise and imports $90 million. What are net exports?
questions.explanation: Net exports equal exports minus imports, or 120 minus 90 equals 30. Positive net exports add to GDP.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Real GDP differs from nominal GDP because real GDP?

options.text: Adjusts for price changes using base-year prices

questions.explanation: Real GDP values output at base-year prices to remove inflation. It still includes services and government spending.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Nominal output rose 8% while prices rose 5%. What happened to real output?

options.misconception: subtracts price change from 100 not from nominal

questions.explanation: Approximately, real growth equals nominal growth minus inflation, or 8% minus 5% equals 3%.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The GDP deflator is best described as?

options.text: A measure of nominal GDP only
A consumer price index for urban households
A price index for all domestically produced output
A ratio of exports to imports

questions.explanation: The GDP deflator covers all domestically produced goods and services, unlike CPI which covers consumer baskets.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Nominal GDP is $400 million and real GDP is $320 million. What is the GDP deflator?
questions.explanation: The deflator equals nominal GDP divided by real GDP times 100, or 400/320*100 equals 125.
questions.hint: Divide nominal by real, then times 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The GDP deflator rises from 110 to 121. What is the inflation rate?
questions.explanation: Inflation is the percentage change, or (121-110)/110*100 equals 10%. The deflator change measures price growth.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.stem: Explain why rising real GDP per person may still not mean better welfare for club members.

answer.exemplar: Real GDP per person ignores inequality, leisure, environmental quality, and non-market activity, so gains may not reach everyone or improve well-being.

questions.explanation: GDP omits distribution, leisure, and externalities, so higher output per person does not guarantee welfare gains.
questions.hint: GDP misses distribution and non-market factors.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Real GDP is $200 million and the club's member population is 50,000. What is real GDP per person?
questions.explanation: Divide real GDP by population, or 200,000,000 / 50,000 equals 4,000. This measures average output per person.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The income approach to GDP sums which items?
questions.explanation: The income approach adds factor incomes: wages, rent, interest, and profit. It equals GDP by identity.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Why might GDP figures for a sports district contain measurement error?

options.text: Informal and unreported activity is missed

questions.explanation: Unreported informal activity escapes measurement, creating error. Other options misstate accounting rules.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain the difference between national income and gross domestic product.

answer.exemplar: GDP measures output produced domestically, while national income measures income earned by a nation's residents, including abroad.

questions.explanation: GDP is geographic; national income is resident-based and includes net factor income from abroad.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: GNP for a sports club's home country includes output produced?

options.text: By the country's residents anywhere in the world

questions.explanation: GNP measures output by a country's residents regardless of location. GDP is the location-based measure.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Disposable personal income is national income minus?

options.misconception: includes taxes not borne by persons

questions.explanation: DPI equals personal income minus personal taxes. It is the income available for spending or saving.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A member's disposable income is $60,000 and consumption is $45,000. What is personal saving?
questions.explanation: Personal saving equals disposable income minus consumption, or 60,000 minus 45,000 equals 15,000.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Disposable income is $80,000 and saving is $12,000. What is the personal saving rate?
questions.explanation: The saving rate is saving divided by disposable income, or 12,000/80,000 equals 0.15 or 15%.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain the paradox of thrift in a sports-club economy.

answer.exemplar: If all members try to save more at once, aggregate demand falls, reducing income so total saving may not rise, illustrating the paradox of thrift.

questions.explanation: Collective saving reduces demand and income, so intended saving may not materialize. This is the paradox of thrift.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The marginal propensity to consume is the fraction of?

options.misconception: confuses with marginal propensity to import

questions.explanation: MPC is the share of an additional dollar of income that is consumed. MPS is the share saved.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The marginal propensity to save equals?

options.text: Total saving divided by total income

questions.explanation: Since additional income is either consumed or saved, MPS = 1 - MPC. Average ratios differ.
questions.hint: Income is split between C and S.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: If the MPC rises, what happens to the spending multiplier?

options.misconception: ignores the MPC in the formula

questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so a higher MPC raises the multiplier. More spending rounds boost output.
questions.hint: Multiplier uses MPC in the denominator.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: With an MPC of 0.8, what is the spending multiplier?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC) = 1/0.2 = 5. Each round of spending adds to output.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Explain how leakages reduce the spending multiplier in a sports-club economy.

answer.exemplar: Savings, taxes, and imports leak spending out of the circular flow, so each round adds less output and the multiplier shrinks.

questions.explanation: Leakages withdraw spending from the circular flow, reducing the multiplier below the simple 1/(1-MPC).

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The balanced budget multiplier is approximately?
questions.explanation: With equal changes in spending and taxes, the net multiplier is about 1. Spending raises output more than taxes reduce it.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: With an MPC of 0.75, what is the tax multiplier?
questions.explanation: The tax multiplier is -MPC/(1-MPC) = -0.75/0.25 = -3. A tax cut of 1 raises output by 3.
questions.hint: Use negative MPC over (1 minus MPC).

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: To move from GDP to national income, one subtracts?

options.misconception: confuses national income with disposable income

questions.explanation: National income equals GDP minus depreciation and net indirect taxes, plus net factor income from abroad.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: An index value of 132 is rebased to a new base year value of 100. What is the rebased index if the old base was 110?
questions.explanation: Rebase by multiplying by 100/110, so 132*100/110 equals 120. The new base year is set to 100.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Sector value added is $50 million for manufacturing and $30 million for services. What is total value added?
questions.explanation: Total value added is the sum across sectors, or 50 + 30 = 80 million. This equals GDP by the value-added approach.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Real GDP grows 4% and population grows 1%. What is approximate real GDP per person growth?
questions.explanation: Approximately, per-person growth equals GDP growth minus population growth, or 4% minus 1% equals 3%.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A club claims 10% output growth, but prices rose 6%. What is real growth approximately?
questions.explanation: Real growth is approximately nominal growth minus inflation, or 10% minus 6% equals 4%.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: With MPC 0.8 and marginal propensity to import 0.1, what is the open-economy multiplier?
questions.explanation: The open-economy multiplier is 1/(1-MPC+MPI) = 1/(1-0.8+0.1) = 1/0.3 = 3.33. Imports add a leakage.
questions.hint: Use 1 divided by (1 minus MPC plus MPI).

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: In a closed economy, investment equals?
questions.explanation: In a closed economy, saving equals investment by identity. This links the financial and real sides.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Reading a growth claim against prices

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Growth that survives a deflator check
questions.stem: Explain why a growth claim must be checked against the deflator before accepting it.

answer.exemplar: Nominal growth may just reflect rising prices, so deflating reveals whether real output actually increased.

questions.explanation: Without adjusting for prices, nominal growth can overstate real gains. The deflator separates price from quantity changes.
